key_terms.meaning: Light and matter show wave behaviour (interference, diffraction) and particle behaviour (photons, electrons).
Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2, where ħ = h/(2π) and h is Planck constant; position and momentum cannot both be exact.
ψ(x,y,z,t) describes a quantum state; |ψ|² gives probability density.
E<sub>n</sub> = n²h²/(8mL²), n = 1,2,3,...; m = mass, L = box length, h = Planck constant.
Z<sub>eff</sub> = Z − S, the nuclear charge felt by an electron after screening S.
Rules that estimate the screening constant S from inner and same-shell electrons.
An orbital formed by linear combination of atomic orbitals over a molecule.
Bond order = (N<sub>b</sub> − N<sub>a</sub>)/2, where N<sub>b</sub> and N<sub>a</sub> are bonding and antibonding electrons.
Energy gap between the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals.
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a solid or solution.
Delocalised valence electrons attract a lattice of positive metal ions.
An ion or molecule that donates an electron pair to a metal centre.
Number of donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal ion.
EAN = Z<sub>metal</sub> − oxidation state + 2 × coordination number for two-electron donors; Z<sub>metal</sub> is atomic number.
Stable organometallic complexes often have 18 valence electrons around the metal, filling nine bonding MOs.
Energy separation Δ between d-orbital sets produced by ligands in a complex.
An electron jump between split d orbitals that can absorb visible light and give colour.
Weak attraction due to one or more unpaired electrons with a net magnetic moment.
Small, highly charged, weakly polarisable species that prefer ionic bonding.
Hard acids prefer hard bases and soft acids prefer soft bases; hard–hard and soft–soft pairs are stable.

takeaways: Light and electrons show both wave and particle behaviour; the uncertainty principle limits simultaneous position and momentum knowledge.
The Schrödinger equation gives allowed wavefunctions and quantised energies; particle-in-a-box energy rises as n²/L².
Inner electrons screen the nucleus, so Z<sub>eff</sub> controls size, ionisation energy and electronegativity trends.
MO theory fills bonding and antibonding orbitals; bond order predicts bond strength and magnetism.
Conjugated π systems such as butadiene and benzene have delocalised MOs; benzene's filled bonding shell gives aromatic stability.
Ionic, covalent, metallic and hydrogen bonding produce different melting points, conductivity and solubility.
Coordination compounds are counted by coordination number, oxidation state, EAN and the 18-electron rule.
Crystal field splitting explains colour, magnetism and ligand-field preferences in transition metal complexes.
HSAB predicts stable acid–base pairs: hard with hard, soft with soft.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine a model with a named example: derive box or MO energies, calculate Z<sub>eff</sub>, draw CFT splittings, compute magnetic moments, and use EAN, 18-electron counting and HSAB to justify stability.

bank.q: Explain wave–particle duality and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Give the de Broglie relation and the uncertainty relation, and state why these effects are not seen for a cricket ball.
outline: de Broglie λ = h/p; photon energy E = hν
double-slit evidence for electrons and light
macroscopic action is large, so uncertainty is negligible

bank.q: Set up the Schrödinger equation for a particle in a one-dimensional box of length L. Solve for ψ<sub>n</sub> and E<sub>n</sub>, and sketch the first three wavefunctions.
Define effective nuclear charge. State Slater's rules and use them to estimate Z<sub>eff</sub> for the 3s electron of Na and the 3p electron of Cl.
Explain how molecular orbitals are formed from atomic orbitals. Draw the MO diagrams of N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>, and give bond order and magnetism.
outline: σ and π bonding and antibonding MOs
two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals

bank.q: Construct the π molecular orbitals of 1,3-butadiene and benzene. Mark nodes, HOMO and LUMO, and explain why benzene is unusually stable.
outline: four p orbitals give four π MOs in butadiene
nodes increase from zero to three
benzene gives six π MOs; filled bonding shell

bank.q: Compare ionic, covalent, metallic and hydrogen bonding in solids. Relate each type to melting point, electrical conductivity and solubility, with one example.
outline: ionic lattice: high melting point, conducts when molten or aqueous
covalent network: hard, high melting point, insulator
hydrogen bonding: weak, low melting point

bank.q: For [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> and [Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>], find the metal oxidation state, coordination number, EAN and 18-electron count.
outline: count ligand donations and metal d electrons

bank.q: Draw the crystal field splitting of d orbitals in octahedral, tetrahedral and square planar complexes. Calculate CFSE for high-spin and low-spin d<sup>4</sup> octahedral cases.
outline: square planar: four lower, one upper
high-spin d<sup>4</sup>: CFSE = −0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>; low-spin d<sup>4</sup>: CFSE = −1.6Δ<sub>o</sub> plus pairing energy

bank.q: Explain why [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is blue and paramagnetic. Calculate its spin-only magnetic moment.
outline: Cu<sup>2+</sup> is d<sup>9</sup> with one unpaired electron
observed colour is complementary to absorbed light

bank.q: Use HSAB to predict whether Ag<sup>+</sup> binds F<sup>−</sup> or I<sup>−</sup> more strongly, and whether Fe<sup>3+</sup> binds OH<sup>−</sup> or I<sup>−</sup> more strongly. Explain.
outline: polarisability and covalent versus ionic character

bank.q: O<sub>2</sub> is paramagnetic although its Lewis structure has no unpaired electrons. Use molecular orbital theory to explain this, and compare the prediction with valence bond theory.
outline: MO filling gives two unpaired electrons in π*

bank.q: Analyse the trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity across Period 3 using Z<sub>eff</sub> and Slater's rules. Explain any anomaly.
outline: radius decreases; ionisation energy generally increases
anomalies from subshell shielding and electron pairing

bank.q: Compare cisplatin and Wilkinson's catalyst using coordination number, geometry, metal oxidation state, ligand field and HSAB ideas. Why is cisplatin useful in medicine and Wilkinson's catalyst useful in hydrogenation?
outline: cisplatin: Pt(II), d<sup>8</sup>, square planar, CN 4
Wilkinson: Rh(I), square planar, CN 4, 16-electron cycle
cisplatin binds DNA and is an anticancer drug

bank.q: Using CFT, the 18-electron rule and HSAB, explain why [Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>] is tetrahedral and stable while [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is square planar and diamagnetic.
outline: d<sup>8</sup> square planar configuration is diamagnetic

glossary.def: The property that light and matter show both wave-like and particle-like behaviour depending on the experiment.
The rule that Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2, where ħ = h/(2π), so position and momentum cannot both be exact at the same time.
A mathematical function ψ that describes the state of a quantum system; |ψ|² gives probability density.
The quantity |ψ|², which gives the probability per unit volume of finding a particle at a point.
A model of a particle confined between two impenetrable walls, giving E<sub>n</sub> = n²h²/(8mL²).
The net positive charge felt by an electron after other electrons screen the nucleus, Z<sub>eff</sub> = Z − S.
A set of empirical rules used to estimate the screening constant S for an electron in an atom.
The minimum energy needed to remove one electron from a gaseous atom or ion.
The tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract shared electrons to itself.
An orbital that belongs to a whole molecule and is built from a linear combination of atomic orbitals.
Half the difference between bonding and antibonding electrons in a molecule.
The highest occupied molecular orbital in a molecule.
The lowest unoccupied molecular orbital in a molecule.
The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A bond formed by sharing one or more pairs of electrons between atoms.
A bonding model in which delocalised valence electrons hold together a lattice of positive metal ions.
A strong dipole–dipole attraction in which H bonded to N, O or F interacts with a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
An ion or molecule that donates an electron pair to a metal ion to form a coordination bond.
The number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal ion.
The charge an atom would have if all its bonds were treated as ionic, assigned by electron counting rules.
Effective atomic number, the electron count around a metal centre calculated from the metal atomic number, oxidation state and ligand donations.
The rule that many stable organometallic complexes have 18 valence electrons around the metal.
The separation of d-orbital energies caused by the electrostatic field of ligands in a complex.
An ordered list of ligands by their ability to split d orbitals; strong-field ligands give larger Δ.
Weak attraction of a substance into a magnetic field due to one or more unpaired electrons.
The principle that hard acids prefer hard bases and soft acids prefer soft bases.
